reason: The sources provide enough factual claims regarding Olympus Mons to support a 45-second script.
story: On Mars sits Olympus Mons, the largest volcano in the solar system. It towers roughly three times the height of Mount Everest and spreads about as wide as the state of Arizona. Yet if you stood on its slopes, you wouldn't even know you were on a mountain. Because its shield volcano profile has an average slope of just five percent, the ground appears as a gently sloping plain stretching to a horizon a mere three kilometers away. Its summit, featuring six nested calderas up to three kilometers deep, remains completely out of view. Instead of a soaring peak, visitors would experience an immense regional landscape, complete with a basal cliff reaching up to nine kilometers high in places.
angle: Standing on the tallest mountain in the solar system, you wouldn't even know you were on a mountain.

claims.claim: Olympus Mons is the largest volcano in the solar system.
Olympus Mons stands approximately 21 to 25 kilometers high.
Olympus Mons is roughly three times the height of Mount Everest.
The volcano's width is about 600 kilometers, comparable to the size of Arizona, Italy, or the Philippines.
The average slope of the volcano's flanks is about 5 percent.
The geometric horizon for a standing observer on Mars is a mere 3 kilometers away.
The summit features six nested calderas forming an irregular depression.
The caldera complex at the peak is up to 3.2 kilometers deep.
The outer edge of the volcano consists of an escarpment or cliff up to 8 or 9 kilometers tall in places.
The last eruption of Olympus Mons occurred roughly 25 million years ago.
Mariner 9 confirmed Nix Olympica as a volcano when it arrived in orbit in 1971.
Giovanni Schiaparelli observed Nix Olympica with a telescope in the late 19th century.

disputed: Exact height measurements vary depending on the chosen reference datum (such as areoid versus local plains), ranging between 21 and 27 kilometers; scripts should use general rounded comparisons like 'roughly three times the height of Everest'.
